name: Phlebotomy Technician Preparation
objectives: Using the official NHA page and your state health department's page, write a plan for a phlebotomy training program, the supervised draws required and a certification exam date, with every requirement checked on an official page
Given a practice patient and a lab order, confirm the patient with two identifiers and match the order before any draw, stopping every time something does not match
Given a set of tube colors and your program's chart, put the tubes in the order of draw, with no tube out of order

chapters.name: Chapter 1: The job, the patient and the tubes

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The job, training and certification
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a plan for a training program, supervised draws and a certification exam.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official NHA page and your state health department's page, you will write a plan for a phlebotomy training program, the supervised draws required and a certification exam date, with every requirement checked on an official page.
A phlebotomy technician collects blood from patients for lab tests and blood donation. The job needs careful steps, a calm manner with nervous patients, and strict safety.
Most people start with a phlebotomy training program at a community college, adult school or career school. You learn on training arms first, then do draws on real people with an instructor watching. This hands-on part cannot be learned online.
Certification: one common choice is NHA's Certified Phlebotomy Technician (CPT). NHA asks for a high school diploma or GED (or one coming soon), a training program or supervised work experience, and proof of at least 30 venipunctures and 10 capillary (finger or heel) sticks on live people. Other groups, such as ASCP, also certify phlebotomists; check their official pages.
Some states set their own rules. California, for example, issues state phlebotomy certificates through the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) and also requires a national exam from an approved group. Check your state health department before you choose a program. Rules and fees change, so read the official pages.
Step by step:
- Find two phlebotomy training programs near you.
- Ask each: how many supervised draws do students do, and which certification does it prepare you for?
- Read the certification's official page for its current requirements.
- Check your state health department for state rules.
- Write target dates: start of training, end of training, exam.
Words to know:
- Phlebotomy: taking blood from a person for testing or donation.
- Venipuncture: putting a needle into a vein to collect blood.
- Capillary stick: a small puncture of the finger or heel to collect a few drops of blood.
- Training arm: a practice model of an arm used to learn draws safely.
Official sources:
- NHA: Certified Phlebotomy Technician (CPT)
- California Department of Public Health: Phlebotomy certificate
Try it now: Write a one-page plan: two training programs near you (name, length, supervised draws, which certification they prepare you for), the certification you will aim for and its requirements from the official page, your state's rules, and three target dates.
You can now say what a phlebotomy technician does, how training works, what NHA's CPT asks for, and where to check your state's rules.

check.q: Where do you learn to actually draw blood?
options: In an approved training program, with an instructor watching
check.why: Draws are learned only in a supervised program, first on training arms.

check.q: What does NHA's CPT ask for, besides training or work experience?
options: Proof of supervised venipunctures and capillary sticks on live people
check.why: NHA asks for proof of at least 30 venipunctures and 10 capillary sticks.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The right patient and the right order
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Confirm the patient with two identifiers and match the lab order before any draw.
This lesson builds toward: Given a practice patient and a lab order, you will confirm the patient with two identifiers and match the order before any draw, stopping every time something does not match.
The most important step happens before the needle: making sure you have the right patient. A sample from the wrong person can lead to the wrong treatment.
Use at least two identifiers, usually full name and date of birth. Ask the patient to say them ("Please tell me your full name and date of birth"), instead of asking "Are you John Smith?", because nervous or confused people may just say yes. In a hospital, also check the ID band against the order.
Then read the lab order (requisition): which tests, any special instructions such as fasting or a set time, and which tubes are needed. If the name, date of birth or anything else does not match, stop and ask your supervisor. Never guess.
Privacy (HIPAA): the order shows private health information. Keep it out of sight, speak quietly, and talk about the tests only with the patient and staff who need to know.
Step by step:
- Introduce yourself and explain what you will do.
- Ask the patient to say their full name and date of birth.
- Compare them with the order (and the ID band in a hospital).
- Check the tests, the tubes and any special instructions such as fasting.
- If anything does not match, stop and ask your supervisor.
Words to know:
- Patient identifiers: details such as full name and date of birth used to make sure you have the right person.
- Requisition: the lab order that lists the patient and the tests to collect.
- Fasting: not eating (and sometimes not drinking anything but water) for a set time before a test.
- HIPAA: the federal law that protects the privacy of health information.
Official sources:
- HHS: HIPAA for professionals (Privacy Rule)
Try it now: Role play with a friend, no needles. Your friend plays a patient with a made-up name and birthday; you hold a made-up lab order with one detail different. Introduce yourself, ask them to say their name and date of birth, compare with the order, and say out loud what you do when it does not match.
You can now identify a patient with two identifiers, check the lab order, stop when something does not match, and keep the information private.

check.q: What is the best way to confirm who the patient is?
options: Ask the person in the waiting room
Ask them to say their full name and date of birth
check.why: Having the patient say two identifiers avoids a nervous "yes" to the wrong name.

check.q: The date of birth on the order does not match what the patient says. What do you do?
options: Change the date on the order
check.why: Any mismatch stops the draw until it is sorted out.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Tubes and the order of draw
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Put a set of tubes in the order of draw using your program's chart.
This lesson builds toward: Given a set of tube colors and your program's chart, you will put the tubes in the order of draw, with no tube out of order.
Tubes have colored caps that tell you what is inside. Some have additives that stop blood from clotting; others help it clot. If additive from one tube gets carried into the next, it can change the test results.
That is why labs follow an order of draw, based on a lab standard from CLSI. A common order is: 1) blood culture bottles, 2) light blue (sodium citrate), 3) red or gold (serum tubes, with or without gel), 4) green (heparin), 5) lavender or purple (EDTA), 6) gray (sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate).
Cap colors can differ between tube makers, and labs can have extra tubes, so always use your program's or lab's own chart. Many students learn a memory line for the order and practice it until it is automatic.
Tubes with additives are gently turned upside down and back (inverted) several times right after filling, as the tube maker says. Never shake them.
Words to know:
- Additive: a chemical inside a tube that stops clotting or helps blood clot.
- Order of draw: the set order for filling tubes so additives do not carry into the next tube.
- Serum: the liquid part of blood after it clots.
- Invert: to turn a tube gently upside down and back.
- CLSI: the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute, a group that writes lab standards.
Try it now: Cut six slips of paper and color or label them: gray, red, blood culture, lavender, light blue, green. Mix them up and put them in the order of draw. Do it five times, faster each time. Check your answer against the order in this lesson, and later against your program's chart.
You can now put common tubes in the order of draw, say why the order matters, and invert tubes gently after filling.

check.q: In the common order of draw, which comes first?
check.why: Blood cultures are drawn first so they stay sterile.

check.q: Why is there an order of draw?
options: So additives from one tube do not get into the next
So the patient sees nice colors
check.why: Additive carried into the next tube can change the test results.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: The draw, safety and specimens

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The steps of a routine blood draw
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Put the steps of a routine venipuncture in order and name when to stop.
This lesson builds toward: Given the steps of a routine venipuncture out of order, you will put the steps in order and name when to stop the draw, with no step missing.
This lesson teaches the steps so you know them before your training program. You will do them only with an instructor watching. Never practice on a person outside a supervised program.
The main steps: identify the patient and check the order; wash your hands and put on gloves; position the patient's arm; apply the tourniquet and choose a vein (the median cubital vein in the bend of the elbow is often the first choice); clean the site and let it air dry; insert the needle at a shallow angle; fill the tubes in the order of draw; release the tourniquet; remove the needle and activate the safety device; apply pressure with gauze; label the tubes in front of the patient; clean up and check on the patient.
Many programs teach not to leave a tourniquet on longer than about one minute, because it can change test results. Follow your program's rules.
Know when to stop: the patient feels faint or passes out, a swelling (hematoma) forms quickly, the patient feels sharp, shooting or electric pain, or the patient asks you to stop. Remove the tourniquet and needle, apply pressure, keep the patient safe and get help.
Step by step:
- Identify the patient and check the order.
- Wash hands and put on gloves.
- Position the arm and apply the tourniquet.
- Choose the vein, then clean the site and let it dry.
- Insert the needle and fill the tubes in the order of draw.
- Release the tourniquet, remove the needle and activate the safety device.
- Apply pressure with gauze.
- Label the tubes in front of the patient, clean up and check on the patient.
Words to know:
- Tourniquet: a band tied around the arm to make veins easier to find.
- Median cubital vein: a vein in the bend of the elbow that is often the first choice for a draw.
- Hematoma: a swelling of blood under the skin.
- Syncope: fainting: a short loss of consciousness.
Try it now: No needles. Write the eight steps of a routine draw on eight cards, mix them up and put them in order. Then, on the back of the last card, write the four signs that mean stop the draw, and what you do next.
You can now list the steps of a routine venipuncture in order and say when to stop a draw and what to do.

check.q: Which step comes right before cleaning the site?
options: Applying the tourniquet and choosing the vein
check.why: You find the vein first, then clean the site and let it dry.

check.q: During a draw the patient says they feel faint. What do you do?
options: Stop the draw, keep them safe and get help
check.why: Feeling faint is a sign to stop: tourniquet and needle out, pressure, keep the patient safe, get help.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Infection control and sharps safety
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the right infection control and sharps safety step in practice situations.
This lesson builds toward: Given practice safety situations, you will choose the right infection control and sharps safety step, getting every situation right.
Blood can carry germs such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV, called bloodborne pathogens. OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard requires employers to have an exposure control plan, offer the hepatitis B vaccine, train workers, provide protective equipment and use safer needle devices.
Your habits: clean your hands before and after every patient and when you take off gloves; wear new gloves for each patient; use needles with a safety device and activate it right away; put used needles straight into a sharps container, never recap them by hand, and never let the container get overfilled.
If you get a needlestick or blood on your skin or in your eyes: wash the area with soap and water (flush eyes with water), and report it to your supervisor right away so you can get checked. Do not wait.
Step by step:
- Clean hands before and after each patient.
- New gloves for each patient.
- Activate the safety device right after the needle comes out.
- Drop the needle straight into the sharps container; never recap by hand.
- Exposure: wash or flush, then report right away.
Words to know:
- Bloodborne pathogens: germs in blood that can cause disease, such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.
- OSHA: the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the federal agency for workplace safety.
- Sharps container: a hard, labeled box for used needles and other sharp items.
- PPE: personal protective equipment, such as gloves.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Bloodborne pathogens and needlestick prevention
Try it now: Practice only. For each situation, write the right step: (1) you finish one patient and the next one sits down, (2) the needle is out of the vein, (3) the sharps container is full to the line, (4) you feel a stick through your glove from a used needle. Answers: clean hands and new gloves; activate the safety device and put it in the sharps container; close it and get a new one; wash the area and report it right away.
You can now choose the right infection control and sharps safety step and say what to do after an exposure.

check.q: What do you do with a used needle?
options: Activate the safety device and put it straight into the sharps container
Put it in the regular trash
Lay it on the tray for later
check.why: Safety device on and straight into the sharps container prevents needlesticks.

check.q: You get a needlestick from a used needle. What is first?
options: Hide it so you are not blamed
Wash the area with soap and water and report it right away
Put a bandage on and forget it
check.why: Wash, then report right away so you can be checked quickly.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Labeling and handling specimens, and your checklist
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Decide whether a specimen is labeled and handled well enough for the lab to accept it.
This lesson builds toward: Given practice specimens, you will decide whether each specimen is labeled and handled well enough for the lab to accept it, spotting every reason for rejection.
A perfect draw is wasted if the lab cannot use the sample. Labs reject specimens that are unlabeled or mislabeled, in the wrong tube, not filled enough, clotted when they should not be, hemolyzed (red blood cells broken, often from a draw that was too rough or shaken tubes), or not kept at the right temperature or time.
Label every tube in front of the patient, right after the draw, never before. Follow your lab's rules for what goes on the label, usually the patient's full name, date of birth or ID number, the date and time, and your initials. Then check the label against the order one more time.
Send specimens the way your lab says: some go on ice, some are kept from light, some must reach the lab within a set time. Keep the patient's information private on the way.
Now make your final task: your own pocket checklist, plus your training and exam plan.
Step by step:
- Label each tube in front of the patient, right after the draw.
- Include what your lab requires: name, date of birth or ID, date, time, your initials.
- Check the labels against the order.
- Handle and send the tubes the way the lab says (ice, light, time).
- Report any problem instead of sending a bad sample.
Words to know:
- Specimen: a sample, such as a tube of blood, sent to the lab.
- Hemolysis: when red blood cells break open, which can ruin some test results.
- Rejected specimen: a sample the lab will not test, so the patient must be drawn again.
Try it now: Final task. Make a pocket checklist for a routine draw: patient ID and order check, hand hygiene and gloves, order of draw, the steps of the draw, when to stop, sharps disposal, labeling in front of the patient, handling and cleanup. On the back, write your plan: training program, certification exam, your state's rules and target dates. Use no real patient information.
You can now label and handle specimens so the lab can use them, spot reasons for rejection, and use your own checklist and plan.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Training and exam plan No program or exam named, or requirements guessed. Names a training program, a certification exam and its requirements from the official page, the state's rules and target dates. Compares two programs, including how many supervised draws each gives. Patient ID and order The checklist skips patient ID or the order check. Starts with two identifiers said by the patient and a check of the order, with "stop if it does not match". Also covers the ID band in a hospital and special instructions such as fasting. Order of draw Tubes missing or out of order. All tubes in the correct order from the program's or lab's chart. Adds the reason the order matters and to invert tubes gently. Steps and stop signs Steps missing or out of order, or no stop signs. All steps in order, with the signs that mean stop the draw. Adds what to do for a fainting patient. Safety No hand hygiene, gloves or sharps step. Hand hygiene, new gloves, safety device, sharps container and what to do after an exposure. Notes never recapping by hand and not overfilling the sharps container. Labeling and handling Labels before the draw or away from the patient. Labels in front of the patient after the draw, checks against the order and follows handling rules. Lists three reasons the lab rejects specimens and how to avoid each. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: When do you label the tubes?
options: At the end of your shift
In front of the patient, right after the draw
check.why: Labeling in front of the patient right after the draw prevents mix-ups.

check.q: A tube arrives at the lab with no label. What happens?
options: The lab guesses whose it is
The lab rejects it and the patient must be drawn again
The lab labels it from memory
check.why: Unlabeled specimens are rejected because no one can be sure whose blood it is.
